zh.q: 桌上这些器材各干什么？教材图2.4-1 和图2.4-3 的接法差在哪？
zh.concl: 教材两个演示的接法不同：图2.4-1 是两只灯泡分别串上线圈和可调电阻后并联，再串主回路的 R₁；图2.4-3 是灯泡与线圈并联，回路里只有开关和电源。本课两张图都建，由「接法」开关整张切。自感：线圈自身电流变化时，它产生的变化磁场在它本身激发出感应电动势。
points: 三只线圈只差匝数与铁芯：A 0.2 H / 2.0 Ω、B 2.0 H / 6.0 Ω、C 0.5 H / 30.0 Ω。
教材两张图接法不同：图2.4-1 有 R 与 R₁，图2.4-3 都没有——本课两张都建，用「接法」开关整张切。
两个演示都没有电表，只靠看亮度；要读数就得另把电流传感器串进被观察的灯泡支路（第 4 步）。

zh.q: 两个灯泡规格相同，为什么闭合开关时 A₁ 比 A₂ 慢亮？教材为什么先调 R、再调 R₁？
zh.concl: 自感电动势阻碍（不是阻止）电流增加：线圈电流从 0 慢慢长到稳态 I∞ = 0.2500 A（τ = 0.0972 s，拓展）；A₂ 支路没有线圈，一步到位、还先超亮。稳态时 di/dt = 0、E_L = 0，线圈只剩直流电阻 6.0 Ω——所以「两灯一样亮」等价于 R = R_L，「两灯正常发光」等价于 R₁ = 3.0 Ω。
points: 教材的调节顺序是考点：先调 R 使两灯一样亮（两支路电阻相等），再调 R₁ 使两灯正常发光；顺序反了亮度就说不清。
闭合瞬间 A₂ 先超亮再回落（0.2857 → 0.2500 A），A₁ 从 0 慢慢起来——这就是图2.4-2 那两条反向磁感线的意思。
「慢」不是「到不了」：稳态 0.2500 A 与没有线圈时一样，稳态 E_L = 0，线圈只是一根带 6.0 Ω 电阻的导线。

zh.q: 开关已经断开了，灯泡的电是从哪来的？为什么反而更亮？教材 p.41 那四个问题怎么答？
zh.concl: 断开后线圈本身就是一个电源，电流沿「线圈 → 灯泡」这个唯一还通的回路继续流：灯泡电流由 +0.2500 A 跳到 −0.5000 A（大小 = 原来的线圈电流、方向相反）；线圈自身 6.0 Ω 小于灯泡 12.0 Ω，所以 I_L0 > I_灯0、灯泡比原来更亮（教材 p.43「有时甚至会比开关断开之前更亮」）；这一下的能量全部来自线圈储存的磁场能。
points: 教材 p.41 那四个思考题只提问、不给答案：本课按原文推出——更慢 / 沿「线圈 → 灯泡」/ 方向相反 / 有可能（条件 R_L < R_灯）。
断开后线圈与灯泡串成同一回路，两者电流大小相等、方向相反（i_灯 + i_L = 0）。
L 大只决定「亮多久」，不决定「闪不闪」——线圈 A、B、C 的断电 τ 是 0.0143 / 0.1111 / 0.0119 s（拓展）。

zh.q: 闪亮只有 0.0770 s，眼睛看得见「闪」，看得见「方向」吗？怎么把这段过程留下来？
zh.concl: 指针式电表读不出 0.1 s 级的过程，传感器加计算机能（教材 p.42）；方向反转不是「变暗」，而是电流真的反向——这就是教材 p.42 做一做第 2 条用「测电阻 R 的电流」专门显示的那件事。
points: 曲线与读数、3D 屏幕同源同拍：同一个 tRun、同一个本段峰值。
两条曲线上下镜像，就是「同一回路串联、方向相反」的画面形式。
面积与能量只留到 p.43 的定性说法，本步不数值化。

zh.q: 换一只线圈，灯泡还闪吗？闪得多猛？把电压调大能「救」一只不闪的线圈吗？
zh.concl: 判据 ρ = I_L0/I_灯0 = R_灯/R_L：ρ > 1 才闪。R_L = 2.0 / 6.0 / 30.0 Ω 与灯泡 12.0 Ω 一比就定了。加大电压改不了判据（两只灯并在同一电源上，比值与 U 无关）。L 只决定「亮多久」：断电 τ 是 0.0143 / 0.1111 / 0.0119 s（拓展）。
points: 判据只用电阻比，所以「调大电压」不会把不闪变成闪。
线圈 A 的 36.0000 倍要弹告警：真实灯泡这样闪几下灯丝就烧了——这一步就是本课那条「错误操作 → 后果 → 要求解释」。
线圈 C 是「细线多匝」的反例：L 只有 0.5 H、R_L 30 Ω，τ 反而比 A 还小。

zh.q: 铭牌写 2.0 H，为什么测出来不是 2.0 H？这是「测错了」还是「元件本来就不是标称值」？
zh.concl: 两件不同的事：① 标称不等于实际（元件容差 +13.14 %，不是测错）→ 所以电感必须测（教材 p.42 用传感器测 I-t 曲线正是这个原因）；② 测量本身的误差分两种：分辨率 0.01 A 是「上下跳 ±0.01 A」，只能判「准不准」、判不了「偏大还是偏小」；采样是有方向的——1000 Hz 下第一个采样点在 0.001 s，峰值读数一定偏小（B 0.9 %、A 6.8 %、C 8.1 %，τ 越小偏得越多）。同一个种子永远同一组读数只是软件性质，不是误差分类的依据。
points: 标称不等于实际是元件容差（+13.14 %，在 ±15 % 内），必须测，不能当成算错。
两类偏差分开说：分辨率是 ± 跳动（只能判准不准）；采样峰值有方向、一定偏小（B 0.9 %、A 6.8 %、C 8.1 %）。
两灯稳态 0.2515 / 0.2499 A 差 0.0016 A：真实器材连长「一样亮」都调不到——但这个差别肉眼看不出，要靠读数。

zh.q: 铁芯里没有导线，为什么会有电流、还发热？把整块铁芯切成一叠薄片，为什么就省电了？
zh.concl: 变化的磁场在导体内部直接激起环形电流（不需要导线）；金属有电阻就发热（P = I²R）——冶炼炉、电磁炉要的就是这份热。要减小它是两条路：增大电阻率（硅钢），以及用互相绝缘的硅钢片叠成（把涡流回路切断、每片的回路变小）。
points: 涡流不需要导线：任何导体块，穿过它的磁通量一变就有涡流。
减小涡流靠的是薄片加绝缘层把回路切断，不是「硅钢不导电」。
1/n² 是工程通用式的量化，教材本节没给 → 一律标拓展。

zh.q: 铝管不吸磁，磁体为什么落得那么慢？把管子锯一道裂缝，会变快还是变慢？
zh.concl: 磁体在导体里运动 → 磁通量变化 → 涡流 → 安培力，而安培力总是阻碍运动（教材 p.37 原句）。裂缝把涡流的环形回路切断，阻尼几乎没了，就掉得快（教材 p.39 练习第 3 题、图2.3-15 甲/乙）。教材只给「1 m 不超过 0.5 s」与「过了许久」两个定性量，本课的 3.3639 / 0.9557 s 是课件设定（拓展）。
points: 阻尼不是「让物体停住」，是永远与运动方向反向；没有相对运动就没有阻尼。
自由下落 0.4518 s 与教材「不超过 0.5 s」相容，铝管 3.3639 s 与「许久」相容（数字是设定值）。
铝管不吸磁，起作用的是感应电流，不是磁力吸引。

zh.q: 三只线圈任你挑一只装上，要做到「断开时灯泡闪一下、但灯泡不至于烧掉」——你挑哪只？为什么把电压调大没用？
zh.concl: 没有新结论：把前八步连起来用一遍——判据 ρ = R_灯/R_L、亮度比 = ρ²、与 U 无关、超过 4.0 倍要告警。三只线圈里只有 B 的 ρ 落在 1 < ρ ≤ 2 这个区间。
points: 先算 ρ 再上台：ρ = R_灯/R_L，大于 2 就超过 4.0 倍。
换线圈要重新合上开关充满再断开（断开后再换线圈 → 本段没有峰值，判据不成立）。
判据与 U 无关，所以「调电压」不是解法（第 5 步的结论）。

en.q: What is each piece of equipment on the bench for? How do the circuits in textbook Fig. 2.4-1 and Fig. 2.4-3 differ?
en.concl: The textbook's two demos are wired differently: in Fig. 2.4-1 the two bulbs, one in series with the coil and one with a variable resistor, are in parallel, with R₁ in the main circuit; in Fig. 2.4-3 the bulb is in parallel with the coil and the circuit has only a switch and supply. This lesson builds both, switching the whole circuit with the "Circuit" switch. Self-induction: when the current in a coil changes, its changing magnetic field induces an EMF in the coil itself.
points: The three coils differ only in turns and core: A 0.2 H / 2.0 Ω, B 2.0 H / 6.0 Ω, C 0.5 H / 30.0 Ω.
The textbook's two figures are wired differently: Fig. 2.4-1 has R and R₁, Fig. 2.4-3 has neither. This lesson builds both and switches between them with the "Circuit" switch.
Neither demo has a meter; you just watch brightness. For readings, add a current sensor in series with the bulb branch being watched (step 4).

en.q: The two bulbs are identical. Why does A₁ light more slowly than A₂ when the switch closes? Why does the textbook adjust R first, then R₁?
en.concl: The self-induced EMF opposes (doesn't prevent) the current increase: the coil current grows slowly from 0 to the steady I∞ = 0.2500 A (τ = 0.0972 s, extension); branch A₂ has no coil, so it jumps straight up and overshoots. In steady state di/dt = 0 and E_L = 0, so the coil is just its DC resistance of 6.0 Ω; hence "both bulbs equally bright" means R = R_L, and "both bulbs lit normally" means R₁ = 3.0 Ω.
points: The textbook's adjustment order is tested: first set R so both bulbs are equally bright (equal branch resistances), then set R₁ so both light normally; in the other order the brightness can't be explained.
At the instant of closing A₂ overshoots and settles (0.2857 → 0.2500 A) while A₁ rises slowly from 0; that's what the two opposite field lines in Fig. 2.4-2 mean.
"Slow" doesn't mean "never gets there": the steady 0.2500 A is the same as without a coil, steady E_L = 0, and the coil is just a wire with 6.0 Ω of resistance.

en.q: The switch is already open, so where does the bulb's current come from? Why is it even brighter? How do you answer the four questions on textbook p.41?
en.concl: After opening, the coil itself is a source, and current keeps flowing around the only loop still closed, "coil → bulb": the bulb current jumps from +0.2500 A to −0.5000 A (equal in size to the previous coil current, opposite in direction). The coil's own 6.0 Ω is less than the bulb's 12.0 Ω, so I_L0 > I_bulb0 and the bulb gets brighter than before (textbook p.43: "sometimes even brighter than before the switch was opened"); all the energy for this comes from the magnetic energy stored in the coil.
points: The four thinking questions on textbook p.41 are asked without answers; this lesson derives them from the text: slower / along "coil → bulb" / opposite direction / possibly (if R_L < R_bulb).
After opening, the coil and bulb form one series loop, so their currents are equal in size and opposite in direction (i_bulb + i_L = 0).
A large L only decides "how long it glows", not "whether it flashes": coils A, B and C have switch-off τ of 0.0143 / 0.1111 / 0.0119 s (extension).

en.q: The flash lasts only 0.0770 s. Your eye can see the "flash", but can it see the "direction"? How do you record the process?
en.concl: A needle meter can't read a 0.1 s process, but a sensor with a computer can (textbook p.42); the reversal isn't "dimming" but a genuinely reversed current, which is exactly what item 2 of the textbook's try-it on p.42 shows by "measuring the current through resistor R".
points: The curve, readings and 3D screen share one clock: the same tRun and the same peak for this segment.
The two curves mirroring each other is the picture of "the same series loop, opposite directions".
Area and energy are left at the qualitative statement on p.43; this step doesn't put numbers on them.

en.q: With a different coil, does the bulb still flash? How hard? Can turning up the voltage "rescue" a coil that doesn't flash?
en.concl: Test ρ = I_L0/I_bulb0 = R_bulb/R_L: it flashes only if ρ > 1. Comparing R_L = 2.0 / 6.0 / 30.0 Ω with the bulb's 12.0 Ω settles it. Raising the voltage can't change the test (both are on the same supply, so the ratio doesn't depend on U). L only decides "how long it glows": switch-off τ is 0.0143 / 0.1111 / 0.0119 s (extension).
points: The test only uses the resistance ratio, so "turning up the voltage" won't turn no-flash into flash.
Coil A's 36.0000 times triggers a warning: a real bulb flashing like that a few times would burn out its filament. This step is the lesson's "wrong action → consequence → explain it".
Coil C is the "thin wire, many turns" counterexample: L is only 0.5 H with R_L 30 Ω, and its τ is even smaller than A's.

en.q: The label says 2.0 H. Why doesn't it measure 2.0 H? Is it "measured wrong" or "the component just isn't its nominal value"?
en.concl: Two different things: ① nominal isn't actual (component tolerance +13.14 %, not a measuring mistake) → so inductance must be measured (that's exactly why textbook p.42 measures I-t curves with a sensor); ② measurement error itself comes in two kinds: 0.01 A resolution means "jumping ±0.01 A", which only tells you "how accurate", not "too high or too low"; sampling has a direction: at 1000 Hz the first sample is at 0.001 s, so the peak reading is always too low (B 0.9 %, A 6.8 %, C 8.1 %; the smaller τ, the larger the bias). The same seed always giving the same readings is a software property, not a basis for classifying errors.
points: Nominal not equalling actual is component tolerance (+13.14 %, within ±15 %); it must be measured and isn't a calculation mistake.
Keep the two kinds of deviation apart: resolution is ± jitter (only tells accuracy); the sampled peak has a direction and is always low (B 0.9 %, A 6.8 %, C 8.1 %).
Steady bulb currents of 0.2515 / 0.2499 A differ by 0.0016 A: with real equipment you can't even quite get "equally bright", but the difference is invisible and only shows in the readings.

en.q: There's no wire in an iron core. Why is there current, and why does it heat up? Why does cutting the solid core into a stack of thin sheets save energy?
en.concl: A changing magnetic field drives loop currents directly inside a conductor (no wire needed); metal has resistance, so it heats up (P = I²R); smelting furnaces and induction cookers want exactly this heat. There are two ways to reduce it: raise the resistivity (silicon steel), and stack mutually insulated silicon steel sheets (cutting the eddy loops so each sheet's loop is smaller).
points: Eddy currents need no wire: in any block of conductor, a change in magnetic flux through it causes eddy currents.
Reducing eddy currents works by cutting the loops with thin sheets and insulation, not because "silicon steel doesn't conduct".
1/n² is a general engineering formula the textbook doesn't give in this section → always labeled extension.

en.q: Aluminum isn't magnetic. Why does the magnet fall so slowly? If you saw a slit along the tube, does it fall faster or slower?
en.concl: A magnet moving in a conductor → changing flux → eddy currents → magnetic force, and that force always opposes the motion (textbook p.37). The slit cuts the eddy current loops, so damping almost disappears and it falls fast (textbook p.39 exercise 3, Fig. 2.3-15 a/b). The textbook only gives two qualitative amounts, "no more than 0.5 s for 1 m" and "a long while"; this lesson's 3.3639 / 0.9557 s are lesson settings (extension).
points: Damping doesn't "stop the object"; it always opposes the motion, and with no relative motion there's no damping.
Free fall in 0.4518 s fits the textbook's "no more than 0.5 s", and 3.3639 s in the aluminum tube fits "a long while" (the numbers are settings).
Aluminum isn't magnetic; it's the induced current that acts, not magnetic attraction.

en.q: Pick one of the three coils to fit so that "the bulb flashes on opening, but doesn't burn out". Which one, and why doesn't turning up the voltage help?
en.concl: No new conclusion: chain the first eight steps together: the test ρ = R_bulb/R_L, brightness ratio = ρ², independence from U, and a warning above 4.0 times. Of the three coils, only B has ρ in the range 1 < ρ ≤ 2.
points: Calculate ρ before fitting: ρ = R_bulb/R_L, and above 2 it goes over 4.0 times.
After swapping coils, close the switch again to charge it, then open (swapping after opening → no peak in this segment, so the test can't hold).
The test doesn't depend on U, so "adjusting the voltage" isn't a solution (step 5's conclusion).
